claim: Systemic vascular pressure in vertebrates is regulated by peripheral resistance in tissue capillary beds.
source: Systemic vascular pressure in vertebrates is regulated by a range of factors: one key element of control is peripheral resistance in tissue capillary beds.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about vertebrate cardiovascular physiology in the abstract.

claim: The response of the skin to hypoxia feeds back on cardiovascular parameters including heart rate, arterial pressures, and body temperature.
source: We show that the response of the skin to hypoxia feeds back on a wide range of cardiovascular parameters, including heart rate, arterial pressures, and body temperature.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: This is the first demonstration of a dynamic role for oxygen sensing in a peripheral tissue directly modifying cardiovascular response to hypoxia.
source: These data represent the first demonstration of a dynamic role for oxygen sensing in a peripheral tissue directly modifying cardiovascular response to the challenge of hypoxia.
evidence: This claim is based on the novelty of the findings presented in the manuscript and comparison to existing literature.

claim: Mammalian skin is amongst the most complex of all vertebrate forms of skin.
source: Mammalian skin is amongst the most complex of all the vertebrate forms of skin.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about comparative anatomy.

claim: Acute systemic hypoxia in mice, rats, rabbits, chickens, dogs, sheep and humans causes acute tachycardia and hypertension.
source: Work undertaken over the last 50 years has shown that acute systemic hypoxia in mice, rats, rabbits, chickens, dogs, sheep and humans causes acute tachycardia and hypertension (Korner and Edwards, 1960; Butler, 1967; Yasuma and Hayano, 2000; Campen et al., 2004; Campen et al., 2005; Walsh and Marshall, 2006; Heinonen et al., 2016; Giussani et al., 1993; Fletcher, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Prolonged hypobaric hypoxia in humans causes tachycardia and hypertension.
source: Prolonged hypobaric hypoxia in humans has also been shown to cause tachycardia and hypertension (these studies have primarily been undertaken in high altitude environments or models thereof)(Schultz et al., 2014; Calbet, 2003; Naeije, 2010; Hainsworth et al., 2007; Vogel and Harris, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on high altitude physiology.

claim: The skin has an extensive vasculature that is responsive to shifts in oxygen availability.
source: The skin has an extensive vasculature, which is known to be responsive to shifts in oxygen availability (Durand et al., 1969; Weil et al., 1969; Kuwahira et al., 1993; Minson, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on skin vasculature.

claim: Keratinocytes in low oxygen release nitric oxide to increase blood flow and improve perfusion.
source: Keratinocytes in low oxygen release nitric oxide to increase blood flow and thereby improve perfusion (Cowburn et al., 2013; Pucci et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In both rodents and humans, the basal epidermis is hypoxic relative to the underlying dermal tissue.
source: Of interest, it has been shown that in both rodents and humans the basal epidermis is hypoxic relative to the underlying dermal tissue, and displays constitutive stabilisation of hypoxia inducible transcription factor-(HIF)α proteins (Cowburn et al., 2013; Cowburn et al., 2014; Peyssonnaux et al., 2008; Boutin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The basal epidermis displays constitutive stabilisation of HIFα proteins.
source: Of interest, it has been shown that in both rodents and humans the basal epidermis is hypoxic relative to the underlying dermal tissue, and displays constitutive stabilisation of hypoxia inducible transcription factor-(HIF)α proteins (Cowburn et al., 2013; Cowburn et al., 2014; Peyssonnaux et al., 2008; Boutin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: HIF transcription factors initiate the transcription of multiple genes involved in oxygen homeostasis, including genes that regulate vascularisation and metabolism.
source: HIF transcription factors initiate the transcription of multiple genes involved in oxygen homeostasis, including a number that regulate vascularisation and metabolism (Semenza, 2003; Semenza, 2009; Pouysségur et al., 2006; Formenti et al., 2010; Djagaeva and Doronkin, 2010; Hubbi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on HIF function.

claim: A dichotomous regulation of nitric oxide is conferred by HIF-1α and HIF-2α regulation of the NOS2 and arginase genes.
source: We have previously shown that a dichotomous regulation of nitric oxide is conferred by HIF-1α and HIF-2α regulation of the NOS2 and arginase genes (Semenza, 2003; Jung et al., 2000) and have now documented this in a number of tissues and cell types (Cowburn et al., 2013; Takeda et al., 2010; Branco-Price et al., 2012; Cowburn et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors and others.

claim: The HIF-1α/NOS2 and HIF-2α/arginase pathways strongly influence tissue L-arginine consumption and NO generation.
source: The HIF-1α/NOS2 and HIF-2α/arginase pathways strongly influence tissue L-arginine consumption and NO generation (Cowburn et al., 2013; Takeda et al., 2010; Branco-Price et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Keratinocyte selective deletion of HIF-1α reduces epidermal NO levels.
source: We have also shown that keratinocyte selective deletion of HIF-1α reduces epidermal NO levels, whereas loss of HIF-2α suppresses arginase expression/activity, increasing local concentrations of NO (Cowburn et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: Loss of HIF-2α suppresses arginase expression/activity, increasing local concentrations of NO.
source: We have also shown that keratinocyte selective deletion of HIF-1α reduces epidermal NO levels, whereas loss of HIF-2α suppresses arginase expression/activity, increasing local concentrations of NO (Cowburn et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: In murine skin, cutaneous NO levels are determined by differential HIFα isoform expression which affect both local vascular resistance and systemic blood pressure.
source: Hence, in murine skin, cutaneous NO levels are determined by differential HIFα isoform expression which affect both local vascular resistance and systemic blood pressure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous research cited in the manuscript.

claim: Almost all previous studies on cardiovascular effects of hypoxia have focused on the first ten minutes of the hypoxic response.
source: The literature on the response of animals to systemic hypoxia and its cardiovascular effects is limited almost exclusively to studies under anaesthesia. Hence, almost all previous studies have focused on the first ten minutes of the hypoxic response.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature based on the authors' review.

claim: Radio-telemetry in non-anesthetised non-restrained animals allows a more rigorous evaluation of changes in hemodynamic variables during acclimation to environmental hypoxia.
source: Radio-telemetry in non-anesthetised non-restrained animals allows a more rigorous evaluation of the changes in hemodynamic variables during the acclimation to environmental hypoxia (Kawaguchi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research on methodology.

claim: Systemic hypoxia induces a tri-modal response with an initial tachycardia and hypertensive phase lasting approximately 10 min, followed by a profound drop in heart rate and blood pressure lasting as long as 24 hr, followed by recovery to close to a normoxic state.
source: The work described here demonstrates for the first time that systemic hypoxia induces a tri-modal response: with an initial tachycardia and hypertensive phase that lasts approximately 10 min, followed by an immediate and profound drop in heart rate and blood pressure that can last as long as 24 hr, followed by a recovery to close to a normoxic state.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Peripheral resistance and oxygen sensing in the skin plays an essential role in systemic cardiovascular response to hypoxia.
source: In this context, we show that peripheral resistance and oxygen sensing, in this case in the skin, plays an essential role in this systemic cardiovascular response.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Peripheral tissues can play a fundamental role in cardiovascular adaptation to hypoxia.
source: These data demonstrate that peripheral tissues can play a fundamental role in cardiovascular adaptation to hypoxia.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Resting heart rates were unchanged in K14cre-HIF-1α, K14cre-HIF-2α, K14cre-Arg1, and K14cre-NOS2 mutants relative to wild type controls through diurnal variation.
source: Continuous monitoring of unrestrained, non-anesthetised mice via radio-telemetric catheterization showed that although resting heart rates were unchanged in all mutants relative to wild type controls (n = 7) through diurnal variation (Figure 1A), there was a constitutive hypotensive state in K14cre-HIF-2α mice (n = 7) and NOS2 mutants (n = 6) (Figure 1B) and a strong trend towards a hypertensive state in K14cre-HIF-1α mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: K14cre-HIF-2α mice and K14cre-NOS2 mutants exhibit a constitutive hypotensive state.
source: Continuous monitoring of unrestrained, non-anesthetised mice via radio-telemetric catheterization showed that although resting heart rates were unchanged in all mutants relative to wild type controls (n = 7) through diurnal variation (Figure 1A), there was a constitutive hypotensive state in K14cre-HIF-2α mice (n = 7) and NOS2 mutants (n = 6) (Figure 1B) and a strong trend towards a hypertensive state in K14cre-HIF-1α mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: K14cre-HIF-1α mice show a strong trend towards a hypertensive state.
source: Continuous monitoring of unrestrained, non-anesthetised mice via radio-telemetric catheterization showed that although resting heart rates were unchanged in all mutants relative to wild type controls (n = 7) through diurnal variation (Figure 1A), there was a constitutive hypotensive state in K14cre-HIF-2α mice (n = 7) and NOS2 mutants (n = 6) (Figure 1B) and a strong trend towards a hypertensive state in K14cre-HIF-1α mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cutaneous temperatures in K14cre-Arg-1 mutants are significantly higher than littermate controls.
source: Cutaneous temperatures were also monitored by radiotelemetry (Figure 1C). Here, we saw that cutaneous temperatures in K14cre-Arg-1 mutants was significantly higher than littermate controls and trend lower in HIF-1α mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cutaneous temperatures in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants trend lower than littermate controls.
source: Cutaneous temperatures were also monitored by radiotelemetry (Figure 1C). Here, we saw that cutaneous temperatures in K14cre-Arg-1 mutants was significantly higher than littermate controls and trend lower in HIF-1α mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is no significant difference in physical activity between mutant groups and littermate control mice.
source: Analysis of physical activity showed no significant difference in the movement levels between the mutant groups and littermate control mice, suggesting these differences in temperature do not result from variable activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Differences in skin temperature between mutants and controls do not result from variable activity.
source: Analysis of physical activity showed no significant difference in the movement levels between the mutant groups and littermate control mice, suggesting these differences in temperature do not result from variable activity (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the activity data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: There is an acute cardiovascular response to hypoxia in the first 10-15 min with increased ventilation and a hypoxic pressor reflex.
source: As noted above, the acute cardiovascular response to hypoxia has been described in a number of animal models. As previous investigators have documented, there was an acute response in the first 10–15 min, with increased ventilation (160BrPM to 250BrPM), and a hypoxic pressor reflex, with blood pressures increasing from means of 123/88 mmHg (baseline) to 143/102 mmHg within the first 10 min (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and citations to previous research.

claim: Following the initial response to hypoxia, there is a severe drop in systemic blood pressures at 12% and 10% oxygen levels.
source: Following this brief initial response, there was a severe drop in systemic blood pressures at the 12% and 10% oxygen levels, to means of 87 mmHg SBP and 57 mmHg DBP at 120 min for 10% oxygen (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: Heart rates peak at 13 min in the lowest level of hypoxia, from 606 BPM to 717 BPM, followed by a decline to 285 BPM at 120 min post-transition.
source: Heart rates peak at 13 min in the lowest level of hypoxia, from 606 BPM (baseline) to 717 BPM at the lowest levels of oxygen, followed immediately by a decline to 285 BPM (a 53% drop from baseline) at 120 min post-transition (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Skin temperature rapidly decreased from 33.7°C to 28.9°C 180 mins post hypoxic challenge, suggesting an increase in peripheral vascular resistance.
source: Analysis of subcutaneous temperature has previously been used as an indirect measurement of peripheral vascular resistance(Schey et al., 2009). We found that skin temperature rapidly decreased from 33.7°C (baseline) to 28.9°C (−4.8°C) 180mins post hypoxic challenge (Figure 2G), suggesting an increase in peripheral vascular resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and inference based on cited methodology.

claim: Physical activity declined from 5.3 m/hr to 0.2 m/hr in the 120 min following the introduction of 10% oxygen.
source: Physical activity also declined from 5.3 m/hr to 0.2 m/hr in the 120 min following the introduction of 10% oxygen.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: At 10% oxygen, recovery to 90% of normoxic heart rates and blood pressures occurred in 36 hr in wild type controls.
source: We defined recovery as the point at which the animal reached 90% of heart rates and blood pressures seen at the same time of the diurnal cycle in normoxia; with this definition, recovery occured in 36 hr at 10% oxygen levels in wild type controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and the authors' definition of recovery.

claim: The onset of 10% environmental hypoxia causes a sharper drop in skin temperatures in K14cre-HIF-1α mice than in littermate control animals.
source: As described above and shown in Figure 1, there is a decrease in skin temperature in mice lacking HIF-1α in keratinocytes. In these mice, the onset of 10% environmental hypoxia causes a sharper drop in skin temperatures (Figure 3A) than that seen in littermate control animals, and temperatures of the skin in HIF-1α mutants remain well below those of littermate mice in the second phase of hypoxic response; they do not recover until the restoration of normoxia (for statistical analysis see Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 9A.

claim: Skin temperatures in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants remain well below those of littermate mice in the second phase of hypoxic response and do not recover until the restoration of normoxia.
source: As described above and shown in Figure 1, there is a decrease in skin temperature in mice lacking HIF-1α in keratinocytes. In these mice, the onset of 10% environmental hypoxia causes a sharper drop in skin temperatures (Figure 3A) than that seen in littermate control animals, and temperatures of the skin in HIF-1α mutants remain well below those of littermate mice in the second phase of hypoxic response; they do not recover until the restoration of normoxia (for statistical analysis see Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 9A.

claim: The initial drop in skin temperature during hypoxia is comparable between K14cre-HIF-1α mutant and littermate control mice as shown by infra-red analysis.
source: Infra-red analysis of skin temperature was also used to monitor peripheral vascular perfusion during hypoxic challenge. The initial drop in skin temperature was comparable between K14cre-HIF-1α mutant and littermate control mice, as shown in Figure 3B.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: K14cre-HIF-1α mutants are essentially hypertensive under normoxic conditions, and this hypertension is exaggerated in the first phase of hypoxic response.
source: As described above, the HIF-1α mutants are essentially hypertensive under normoxic conditions, and this hypertension is exaggerated in the first phase of hypoxic response (Figure 3C, for statistical analysis see Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 9B.

claim: In the second phase of hypoxia, K14cre-HIF-1α mutants show a larger drop in systolic and diastolic pressures relative to littermate control mice.
source: However, in the second phase there is a larger drop in systolic and diastolic pressures relative to littermate control mice (Figure 3D, for statistical analysis see Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 9C.

claim: Diastolic pressures in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants begin to elevate in the first hour of hypoxia and gradually increase throughout the 48 hr of hypoxic exposure.
source: This resolves rapidly, and although the subsequent systolic pressures in mutants are similar to those in littermate control animals, the diastolic pressures in the mutants begin to elevate. This elevated diastolic pressure begins in the first hour of hypoxia, and gradually increases throughout the 48 hr of hypoxic exposure (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Elevation of systolic pressures in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants does not reappear until the animals are restored to normoxia.
source: An elevation in systolic pressures in HIF-1α mutants does not reappear until the animals are restored to normoxia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Elevation of diastolic pressures is indicative of an increase in peripheral resistance.
source: Elevation of diastolic pressures is indicative of an increase in peripheral resistance, and this is consistent with the lowered skin temperatures described above (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an inference based on established physiological knowledge and consistency with observed data.

claim: K14cre-HIF-1α mutants show an increase in heart rate that is likely required to sustain systolic pressures, coinciding with the relative increase in diastolic pressures.
source: In Figure 3E and F, the acute and chronic changes in heart rate in littermate control and mutant animals can be seen (for statistical analysis see Figure 9D and E). The chief difference seen in the HIF-1α mutants is an increase in heart rate that is likely required to sustain systolic pressures; this coincides with the relative increase in diastolic pressures in HIF-1α mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E-F and Figure 9D-E, with inference about the physiological mechanism.

claim: The chronic change in heart rate in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants appears to coincide with an increase in whole-body metabolic activity between 12-36 hr hypoxia.
source: The chronic change in heart rate in HIF-1α mutants appears to coincide with an increase in whole-body metabolic activity between 12–36 hr hypoxia, as determined by VO2 and VCO2 analysis (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Normal metabolic activity in K14cre-HIF-1α mutants is only restored when the animals are returned to normoxia.
source: Normal metabolic activity is only restored when the animals are returned to normoxia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Physical activity is reduced in littermate control and K14cre-HIF-1α mutant animals during the initial 12 hr of hypoxia.
source: Physical activity is reduced in littermate control and mutant animals during the initial 12 hr of hypoxia. Activity slowly increases during the acclimation period, but does not fully recover until the animals are restored to normoxia (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H (note: text refers to Figure 3H but likely means 3I based on figure layout).

claim: Loss of HIF-1α in the epidermis delays the cardiovascular changes that occur in response to hypoxia, correlated with an increase in peripheral resistance and heart rates.
source: Overall, loss of HIF-1α in the epidermis appears to delay the cardiovascular changes that occur in response to hypoxia; this is correlated with an increase in peripheral resistance and in heart rates.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: Hypoxia results in an initial HIF-1α/NOS2/NO mediated increase in vascular diameter and resulting increases in perfusion, followed by a HIF-2α/Arginase-induced reduction of intracellular L-arginine that suppresses NO production and causes vasoconstriction.
source: We have proposed a model for hypoxic responses involving HIF isoform activity and nitric oxide homeostasis in the skin that argues that hypoxia results in an initial HIF-1α/NOS2/NO mediated increase in vascular diameter, and resulting increases in perfusion; followed by a HIF-2α/Arginase-induced reduction of intracellular L-arginine (Cowburn et al., 2013). As L-arginine is necessary for NO production, this would suppress NO production by NO synthases, and ultimately cause vasoconstriction.
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on previous research and current findings.

claim: Animals lacking HIF-2α in the epidermis show elevated skin temperatures in the first 12 hr of hypoxia relative to littermate control animals.
source: This model for HIFα isoform action in hypoxic vascular tissues fits the observations described above for the loss of HIF-1α in the skin. In animals lacking HIF-2α in the epidermis, adaptation of skin temperatures in the first 12 hr of hypoxia follows the predictions of this model (Figure 4A), that is, we see elevated skin temperatures in the HIF-2α mutants relative to littermate control animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Infra-red analysis shows that the recorded drop in skin temperature during hypoxia is significantly less in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants relative to littermate control animals.
source: These data are supported by infra-red analysis of skin temperature during short term hypoxia exposure (Figure 4B). The recorded drop in skin temperature is significantly less in the HIF-2α mutants relative to littermate control animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After 24 hr of hypoxia, skin temperatures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants drop relative to littermate control animals and remain lower for 12 hr before rising again to levels similar to littermate controls.
source: However, after 24 hr, skin temperatures in mutants drop relative to littermate control animals, and remain lower than those of littermate control animals for 12 hr, before rising again to levels similar to those of littermate controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Upon restoration of environmental normoxia, skin temperatures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants return to levels slightly higher than those seen in littermate control animals.
source: Upon restoration of environmental normoxia, skin temperatures in mutants return to levels slightly higher than those seen in littermate control animals, that is, similar to those seen at steady state (for statistical analysis see Figure 9F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: For the first 24 hr of hypoxia, K14cre-HIF-2α mutants show elevated systolic and diastolic pressures that are evident in the first minutes of hypoxic exposure.
source: As shown in Figure 1, mean blood pressures of HIF-2α mutants are significantly lower than those of littermate control animals. For the first 24 hr of hypoxia, HIF-2α mutants show elevated systolic and diastolic pressures that are evident in the first minutes of hypoxic exposure (Figure 4C, [for statistical analysis see Figure 9G] and Figure 4D, [for statistical analysis see Figure 9H]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-D and Figure 9G-H.

claim: At 24 hr of hypoxia, diastolic pressures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants are similar to those seen in littermate control animals, but systolic pressure drops relative to littermate controls.
source: Here again, there is a shift at 24 hr, and although diastolic pressures at that point are similar to those seen in littermate control animals, systolic pressure drops relative to littermate controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Systolic blood pressures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants remain substantially lower than littermate controls until normoxia is restored.
source: The systolic blood pressures remain substantially lower until normoxia is restored, when they return to steady state and mildly hypotensive levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: At the return of normoxia, diastolic pressures in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants rise to levels substantially higher than those seen in littermate control animals for approximately 12 hr.
source: Finally, at the return of normoxia, diastolic pressures rise to levels substantially higher than those seen in littermate control animals for approximately 12 hr, before finally dropping again 24 hr after the restoration of normoxia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Changes in the skin affect both traditionally understood changes in peripheral resistance (altered diastolic pressures) and other changes that can influence systolic pressures.
source: This effect on both systolic and diastolic pressures indicates that changes in the skin affect both traditionally understood changes in peripheral resistance, that is, changes that result in altered diastolic pressures, and other changes that can influence systolic pressures.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on blood pressure changes.

claim: Hypoxia has virtually no effect on heart rate in K14cre-HIF-2α mutant animals.
source: The effect of hypoxia on the heart rate of the epidermal HIF-2α knockout animals is strikingly altered when compared to the effect on littermate control animals. Hypoxia has virtually no effect on heart rate in the HIF-2α mutant animals (Figure 4E, for statistical analysis see Figure 9I); they show a diurnal variation of heart rate that is essentially the same as that seen in animals in normoxic conditions (Figure 4F, for statistical analysis see Figure 9J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F and Figure 9I-J.

claim: K14cre-HIF-2α mutant animals show a diurnal variation of heart rate that is essentially the same as that seen in animals in normoxic conditions.
source: The effect of hypoxia on the heart rate of the epidermal HIF-2α knockout animals is strikingly altered when compared to the effect on littermate control animals. Hypoxia has virtually no effect on heart rate in the HIF-2α mutant animals (Figure 4E, for statistical analysis see Figure 9I); they show a diurnal variation of heart rate that is essentially the same as that seen in animals in normoxic conditions (Figure 4F, for statistical analysis see Figure 9J).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E-F and Figure 9I-J.

claim: Whole-body metabolic activity (VO2 and VCO2) in K14cre-HIF-2α mutant animals is significantly increased above littermate control rates between 12-24 hr hypoxia.
source: Whole-body metabolic activity (VO2 and VCO2) in HIF-2α mutant animals is also significantly increased above littermate control rates between 12–24 hr hypoxia (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Increased metabolic activity in K14cre-HIF-2α mutants does not return to levels seen in littermate control animals until the mice are returned to normoxia.
source: This increased metabolic activity does not return to levels seen in littermate control animals until the mice are returned to normoxia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Activity of K14cre-HIF-2α mutant animals recovers substantially between 12-48 hr of hypoxia, although it does not fully recover until the animals are restored to normoxia.
source: Physical activity, similarly to the patterns described above, is greatly reduced in littermate and mutant animals during the initial 12 hr of hypoxia. However, activity of HIF-2α mutant animals recovers substantially between 12–48 hr, although it does not fully recover until the animals are restored to normoxia (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The crossover seen in skin temperature and blood pressure at 24 hr indicates a phase of adaptation revealed by the HIF-2α deletion, related to a temporally specific action of HIF-2α in the adaptation and response to hypoxia.
source: These results indicate a complex response of the skin to systemic hypoxia, and also demonstrate that that complexity is mirrored in the effect of those responses on the cardiovascular system. The crossover seen in skin temperature and blood pressure at 24 hr also indicates that there is likely a phase of adaptation at that time point revealed by the HIF-2α deletion, and related to a temporally specific action of HIF-2α in the adaptation and response to hypoxia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on temporal patterns.

claim: There is a steep drop in plasma NO metabolites over the first day of hypoxia, followed by a more gradual decline over the following 3 days of exposure.
source: Given the complex role of HIF-2α in the epidermis, and our hypothesis that this could be determined by the differential effect of HIF-1α and HIF-2α on NO homeostasis, we next analysed the overall levels of NO metabolites induced by hypoxia in specific tissues following hypoxic exposure (Figure 5). As can be seen in Figure 5A, there was a steep drop in plasma NO metabolites over the first day of hypoxia, followed by a more gradual decline over the following 3 days of exposure (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Skin shows an initial spike in arginase-1 and -2 expression in the first 24 hr of hypoxia exposure, which then declines.
source: However, as shown in Figure 5B, in skin, and in Figure 5C, in lungs, differing levels of expression of hypoxia-sensitive genes involved in the NO synthesis pathway are evident. Of note, the skin shows an initial spike in arginase-1 and -2 expression in the first 24 hr of exposure, which then declines.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Skin NOS2 expression is marginally higher during the first 24 hr of hypoxia.
source: Skin NOS2 expression over the same time is marginally higher, however.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: In the lung, there is no substantial increase in NOS2 or arginase-1 or -2 expression until after two days of exposure to hypoxia.
source: In the lung there is no substantial increase in NOS2 or arginase-1 or -2 expression until after two days of exposure to hypoxia.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The levels of NO metabolites in the skin and lung reflect the expression levels of arginase and NOS2 mRNA.
source: The levels of NO metabolites seen in the skin and lung reflect the expression levels of arginase and NOS2 mRNA, with an increase seen in the skin at 24 hr and a subsequent decline to baseline levels after 2 days of hypoxia (Figure 5D). This is in contrast to the lung, which shows a gradual decline in NO metabolites at 48–72 hr (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D-E.

claim: Skin shows an increase in NO metabolites at 24 hr and a subsequent decline to baseline levels after 2 days of hypoxia.
source: The levels of NO metabolites seen in the skin and lung reflect the expression levels of arginase and NOS2 mRNA, with an increase seen in the skin at 24 hr and a subsequent decline to baseline levels after 2 days of hypoxia (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The lung shows a gradual decline in NO metabolites at 48-72 hr of hypoxia.
source: This is in contrast to the lung, which shows a gradual decline in NO metabolites at 48–72 hr (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There is a temporal and tissue-specific shift in the expression of NOS2 and Arg-1/-2 in vivo.
source: These data indicate a temporal and tissue-specific shift in the expression of NOS2 and Arg-1/-2 in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on gene expression patterns.

claim: Deletion efficiency of epidermal NOS2 in K14cre+ mice is greater than 98%.
source: To test the hypothesis that keratinocyte HIF-1α/NOS/NO influences shifts in skin temperature, systemic blood pressure and heart rates during exposure to hypoxia, we next generated mice with NOS2 deletions in keratinocytes. Deletion efficiency of epidermal NOS2 in K14cre+ mice was calculated to be greater than 98% in all mice analysed (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Deletion of epidermal NOS2 shows changes in baseline skin temperature and systemic blood pressures similar to those seen in HIF-2α mutant mice.
source: The deletion of epidermal NOS2 shows changes in baseline skin temperature (which is likely correlated with peripheral vascular resistance) and systemic blood pressures similar to those seen in HIF-2α mutant mice, and initial changes in heart rate similar to those seen in HIF-1α mutant mice.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data across different mutant lines.

claim: Deletion of epidermal NOS2 shows initial changes in heart rate similar to those seen in HIF-1α mutant mice.
source: The deletion of epidermal NOS2 shows changes in baseline skin temperature (which is likely correlated with peripheral vascular resistance) and systemic blood pressures similar to those seen in HIF-2α mutant mice, and initial changes in heart rate similar to those seen in HIF-1α mutant mice.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data across different mutant lines.

claim: Epidermal deletion of NOS2 sustains an elevated skin temperature relative to littermate controls for the first 24 hr of hypoxia.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, epidermal deletion of NOS2 sustains an elevated skin temperature relative to littermate controls for the first 24 hr of hypoxia, before returning to levels seen in control mice for the remainder of the recording (for statistical analysis see Figure 9K).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 9K.

claim: K14cre-NOS2 mutant animals display a profound hypotensive phenotype with an apparent decrease in both systolic and diastolic pressures within the first 20 min of hypoxia exposure.
source: In Figure 6C and D, the similarities to the HIF-2α mutant mice are evident, as the K14-NOS2 mutant animals display a profound hypotensive phenotype, with an apparent decrease in both systolic and diastolic pressures within the first 20 min of hypoxia exposure (for statistical analysis see Figure 9L).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C-D and Figure 9L.

claim: The hypotensive state in K14cre-NOS2 mutants is maintained throughout the hypoxic time course.
source: This hypotensive state is maintained throughout the hypoxic time course (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Maximal deflection of systolic pressures (-15 to -20 mmHg) in K14cre-NOS2 mutants occurs between 24-48 hr hypoxic exposure when compared to littermate controls.
source: Maximal deflection of systolic pressures (−15 to −20 mmHg) occurs between 24–48 hr hypoxic exposure when compared to littermate controls (statistical analysis Figure 9M).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 9M.

claim: K14cre-NOS2 mutant heart rate acclimation to hypoxia responds in a similar pattern to HIF-1α mutants, with a profound increase in BPM 120 mins after hypoxia exposure that is maintained throughout the first 24 hr.
source: In contrast, NOS2 mutant heart rate acclimation to hypoxia responds in a similar pattern to the HIF-1α mutants, with a profound increase in BPM 120mins after hypoxia exposure. This is also maintained throughout the first 24 hr of hypoxia exposure (Figure 6E and F [for statistical analysis see Figure 9N and O]).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E-F and Figure 9N-O.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis identified a significant increase in the expression of both NOS1 and NOS3 in K14cre-NOS2 mice exposed to hypoxia when compared to littermate controls.
source: The distinct tensive/cardiac response to hypoxia reported above may be due to a potential compensatory role of NOS1 and NOS3 expression in the skin counteracting the loss of NOS2. RT-qPCR analysis in whole skin samples identified a significant increase in the expression of both NOS1 and NOS3 in K14cre-NOS2 mice exposed to hypoxia (6 hr) when compared to littermate controls (Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The compensatory roles of NOS isoform expression have been previously reported in other animal models of NOS deletion.
source: The compensatory roles of NOS isoform expression have been previously reported in other animal models of NOS deletion (Colton et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Comparative analysis of VEGF-A identified no compensatory expression in K14cre-NOS2 mice.
source: Interestingly, comparative analysis of VEGF-A identified no compensatory expression in K14cre-NOS2 mice (Figure 6H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: K14cre-Arg1 mutant animals display an elevated skin temperature relative to littermate control mice during the first twelve hours of hypoxic exposure, followed by a relative decline at 24 hr.
source: To determine if the complex shifts in skin temperature, blood pressure and heart rate during hypoxia seen in HIF-2α mutant animals were due to HIF-2α regulation of the arginase pathway, we next analysed mice with Arg1 deletions in keratinocytes. As can be seen in Figure 7A, and similarly to what was seen in HIF-2α mutant mice, these animals display an elevated skin temperature relative to littermate control mice during the first twelve hours of hypoxic exposure, followed by a relative decline at 24 hr (for statistical analysis see Figure 9P).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 9P.

claim: K14cre-Arg1 mutants show a small increase in systolic and diastolic pressures for the first 10 min of hypoxia, followed by a decrease in both pressures similar to littermate control animals.
source: In Figure 7B (for statistical analysis see Figure 9Q) it is apparent that there is a small increase in systolic and diastolic pressures for the first 10 min hypoxia, followed by a decrease in both systolic and diastolic pressure. This occurs in a manner similar to that of littermate control animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 9Q.

claim: The recovery of a normotensive state in K14cre-Arg1 mutant mice is somewhat similar to that seen in littermate controls.
source: The recovery of a normotensive state in K14cre-Arg1 mutant mice, is somewhat similar to that seen in littermate controls (Figure 7C)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9R).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 9R.

claim: The effect on heart rate in K14cre-Arg1 mutants is similar to that seen in HIF-2α mutants, with an overall increase relative to the hypoxia-induced decline seen in littermate control animals.
source: However, the effect on heart rate is similar in some regards to that seen in HIF-2α mutants, with an overall increase relative to the hypoxia-induced decline seen in littermate control animals (Figure 7D)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9S), and a more rapid return to the normal pattern of diurnal variation in heart rate (Figure 7E)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9T).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E and Figure 9S-T.

claim: K14cre-Arg1 mutants show a more rapid return to the normal pattern of diurnal variation in heart rate compared to littermate controls.
source: However, the effect on heart rate is similar in some regards to that seen in HIF-2α mutants, with an overall increase relative to the hypoxia-induced decline seen in littermate control animals (Figure 7D)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9S), and a more rapid return to the normal pattern of diurnal variation in heart rate (Figure 7E)(for statistical analysis see Figure 9T).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D-E and Figure 9S-T.

claim: Both VO2 and VCO2 in K14cre-Arg1 mutants substantially increased between 12 and 48 hr of hypoxia, coinciding with heightened physical activity.
source: Metabolic activity of the Arg-1 animals also follows a similar trajectory to that seen in HIF-2α mutant animals. Both VO2 and VCO2 (Figure 7F–G) substantially increased between 12 and 48 hr of hypoxia, and this again coincided with heightened physical activity (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F-H.

claim: The changes seen in Arg-1 mutants are less striking than those seen in HIF-2α mutants, likely due in part to the presence of Arg-2 in the skin of these animals.
source: In each case, the changes seen in Arg-1 mutants were less striking than those seen in HIF-2α mutants, likely due in part to the presence of Arg-2 in the skin of these animals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of experimental data and knowledge of gene expression.

claim: A significant aspect of the HIF-2α-mediated changes in the cardiovascular response to hypoxia may be mediated via its regulation of arginase expression.
source: These data indicate that a significant aspect of the HIF-2α-mediated changes in the cardiovascular response to hypoxia may be mediated via its regulation of arginase expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing HIF-2α and Arg1 mutants.

claim: Resting ventilation rates are similar in HIFα mutant animals relative to littermate controls.
source: We next questioned whether epidermal deletion of HIFα isoforms influenced the basal or hypoxia-induced ventilatory response. Whole-body plethysmography showed that resting ventilation rates are similar in the HIFα mutant animals relative to littermate controls (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: All HIFα mutant mice responded normally to acute hypoxia by increasing ventilation rates.
source: All mice responded normally to acute hypoxia by increasing ventilation rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: K14cre-HIF-1α, K14cre-HIF-2α, and wild type littermate control mice increased their respiratory rate for the initial 10 min of hypoxic exposure, before reducing their ventilation rates 30 min after exposure to hypoxia began.
source: K14cre-HIF-1α, K14cre-HIF-2α, and wild type littermate control mice increased their respiratory rate for the initial 10 min of hypoxic exposure, before reducing their ventilation rates 30 min after exposure to hypoxia began (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: Oxygen partial pressures in the blood were not significantly different from those seen in littermate animals during an acute hypoxic challenge.
source: Oxygen partial pressures in the blood were not significantly different from those seen in littermate animals during an acute hypoxic challenge (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Histological examination showed no discernable differences in the size or number of oxygen sensing cells in the carotid bodies of mutant animals when compared to littermate control mice.
source: Likewise, histological examination of the carotid bodies showed that there were no discernable differences in the size or number of oxygen sensing cells in the mutant animals when compared to those of littermate control mice (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: This is the first detailed investigation of cardiovascular acclimatization to hypoxia in mice over the time frames used in this study.
source: We believe that this is the first detailed investigation of cardiovascular acclimatization to hypoxia in mice over the time frames used here.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on comparison to existing literature.

claim: Previous studies examining cardiovascular hypoxic response have either ended after approximately ten minutes of observation and used anaesthesia, or have involved long term exposures with monitoring after days or weeks of conditioning.
source: Although there have been a number of previous studies examining cardiovascular hypoxic response, these have either ended after approximately ten minutes of observation and used anaesthesia, or have involved long term exposures, with monitoring after days or weeks of conditioning (Campen et al., 2004; Campen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature supported by citations.

claim: Mice exhibited a well-documented elevation of heart rate and blood pressure for the first ten minutes of exposure to hypoxia.
source: We found that mice exhibited a well-documented elevation of heart rate and blood pressure for the first ten minutes of exposure to hypoxia(Campen et al., 2004; Yu et al., 1999; Dematteis et al., 2008; Pearson et al., 2007), but then, experience a dramatic drop in both parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: After the initial elevation, mice experience a dramatic drop in heart rate and blood pressure.
source: We found that mice exhibited a well-documented elevation of heart rate and blood pressure for the first ten minutes of exposure to hypoxia(Campen et al., 2004; Yu et al., 1999; Dematteis et al., 2008; Pearson et al., 2007), but then, experience a dramatic drop in both parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The maximal negative deflection in heart rate and blood pressure was observed at 3 hr post-onset of hypoxic exposure, which coincided with increased peripheral vascular resistance and very low physical activity.
source: The maximal negative deflection in heart rate and blood pressure was observed at 3 hr post-onset of hypoxic exposure, which coincided with increased peripheral vascular resistance, and very low physical activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Cardiovascular parameters were approximately restored to normoxic levels over 45 hr following the maximal negative deflection.
source: Cardiovascular parameters were approximately restored to normoxic levels over the next 45 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The paths of decline and recovery in cardiovascular parameters are graded relative to the degree of hypoxic challenge.
source: These paths of decline and recovery are striking adaptive responses to hypoxia, and they appear to be graded relative to the degree of hypoxic challenge.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data at different oxygen levels.

claim: The processes controlling cardiovascular responses to hypoxia include chemoreceptors and baroreceptors as part of an autonomic nervous system reflex.
source: The processes controlling cardiovascular responses to hypoxia are complex, and include chemoreceptors and baroreceptors as part of an autonomic nervous system reflex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cardiovascular physiology.

claim: Neurally-mediated responses interact with and may frequently mask local tissue effects of hypoxia on cardiovascular responses.
source: These neurally-mediated responses also interact with, and may frequently mask, local tissue effects of hypoxia on cardiovascular responses, making it difficult to dissociate extrinsic and local tissue responses (Bärtsch and Gibbs, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A balance in keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression modulates peripheral vascular resistance.
source: We have previously documented that a balance in keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression modulates peripheral vascular resistance (Boutin et al., 2008), and that this directly affects murine systemic blood pressure; it is also correlated with the tonic tensive state in mildly hypertensive humans (Cowburn et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: Keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression directly affects murine systemic blood pressure.
source: We have previously documented that a balance in keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression modulates peripheral vascular resistance (Boutin et al., 2008), and that this directly affects murine systemic blood pressure; it is also correlated with the tonic tensive state in mildly hypertensive humans (Cowburn et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research by the authors.

claim: Keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression is correlated with the tonic tensive state in mildly hypertensive humans.
source: We have previously documented that a balance in keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression modulates peripheral vascular resistance (Boutin et al., 2008), and that this directly affects murine systemic blood pressure; it is also correlated with the tonic tensive state in mildly hypertensive humans (Cowburn et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research by the authors.

claim: This is the first demonstration that keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression affects the immediate, acute and chronic phases of the cardiovascular response to hypoxia.
source: Here we show for the first time that keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α expression affects the immediate, acute and chronic phases of the cardiovascular response to hypoxia.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Hypoxia immediately heightens sympathetic tone in the skin to increase peripheral vascular resistance.
source: Hypoxia immediately heightens sympathetic tone in the skin to increase peripheral vascular resistance (Simmons et al., 2007; Chalmers and Korner, 1966; Kollai, 1983).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hypoxia increases nitric oxide release from keratinocytes to stimulate vasodilation and act as a neuromodulator of sympathetic activity, dampening vasoconstriction.
source: Hypoxia also increases nitric oxide release from keratinocytes to stimulate vasodilation and act as a neuromodulator of sympathetic activity, dampening vasoconstriction (Ramchandra et al., 2005; Sartori et al., 2005; Hirooka et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The opposing roles of keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α on nitric oxide synthesis suggest divergent effects on sympathetic activity and blood flow in the skin.
source: The opposing roles of keratinocyte HIF-1α and HIF-2α on nitric oxide synthesis (Cowburn et al., 2013) would suggest divergent effects on sympathetic activity and blood flow in this highly vascular tissue.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous research and current findings.

claim: Epidermal HIF-1α has a direct effect on peripheral vascular resistance and the tonic tensive status of the mouse.
source: Epidermal HIF-1α is shown here to have a direct effect on peripheral vascular resistance and the tonic tensive status of the mouse.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claim: In K14cre-HIF-2α mutants, there is a significant increase in heart rate, likely to maintain systolic blood pressure.
source: The opposite cardiovascular relationship is apparent in the HIF-2α mutant mouse. In the case of the HIF-2α mouse, however, there is a significant increase in heart rate, likely to maintain systolic blood pressure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on heart rate and blood pressure.

claim: Epidermal deletion of arginase-1 phenocopied several characteristics of the K14cre-HIF-2α mutant mouse.
source: Epidermal deletion of arginase-1 in this hypoxia acclimation model phenocopied several characteristics of the K14cre-HIF-2α mutant mouse.
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data across different mutant lines.

claim: The effect of arginase-1 deletion is lessened compared to HIF-2α deletion, indicating that other genes controlled by HIF-2α are likely involved in the hypoxic acclimation process.
source: There is an overall lessening of the effect, however, indicating that other genes controlled by HIF-2α are likely involved in the hypoxic acclimation process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of experimental data.

claim: Alterations in peripheral vascular blood flow affect whole body metabolism and physical activity during the acclimation phase to hypoxia.
source: These alterations in peripheral vascular blood flow also appear to affect whole body metabolism and physical activity during the acclimation phase to hypoxia.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on metabolism and activity.

claim: All four epidermal mutant mice demonstrated a similar increase in oxygen consumption during the acclimation phase to hypoxia.
source: Although all four epidermal mutant mice described here demonstrated a similar increase in oxygen consumption during this acclimation phase, only K14cre-HIF-2α and K14cre-arginase-1 mice demonstrated some preservation of physical activity in comparison to wild-type animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Only K14cre-HIF-2α and K14cre-arginase-1 mice demonstrated some preservation of physical activity during hypoxia in comparison to wild-type animals.
source: Although all four epidermal mutant mice described here demonstrated a similar increase in oxygen consumption during this acclimation phase, only K14cre-HIF-2α and K14cre-arginase-1 mice demonstrated some preservation of physical activity in comparison to wild-type animals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The response of peripheral tissue can modulate the animal's overall behaviour during environmental stress.
source: This is intriguing, as it indicates that the response of the peripheral tissue can modulate the animals overall behaviour during environmental stress.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on activity levels.

claim: The data are consistent with cardiopulmonary investigation of patients with germline, heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in HIF-2α, where baseline heart rate and cardiac responses to moderate hypoxia were higher in HIF-2α-gain of function patients compared to control subjects.
source: Interestingly, the data presented here are consistent with cardiopulmonary investigation of patients with germline, heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in HIF-2α, where baseline heart rate and cardiac responses to moderate hypoxia were shown to be higher in the HIF-2α-gain of function patients when compared to control subjects, suggesting an increase in cardiac sympathetic tone (Formenti et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research and comparison to current findings.

claim: Peripheral tissues and their vascular beds form a complex physiological network of oxygen-responsive tissues that influence, and are not just influenced by, central regulators of cardiovascular function.
source: In summary, we present here the first dissection of the murine cardiovascular response to hypoxia, and we present evidence that this response is highly influenced by peripheral vascular responses. This indicates that peripheral tissues, and their vascular beds, form a complex physiological network of oxygen-responsive tissues that influence, and are not just influenced by, central regulators of cardiovascular function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cardiovascular responses to hypoxia are likely a summation of a range of tissue responses, and not solely dictated by central mediators of cardiovascular activity.
source: This interaction amongst tissues indicates that cardiovascular responses to hypoxia are likely a summation of a range of tissue responses, and not solely dictated by central mediators of cardiovascular activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All mice used in the study were in a C57/Bl6J background ascertained by extensive backcrossing and SNP analysis.
source: Targeted deletion of Hif1a (HIF-1α), Epas1 (HIF-2α), Nos2 (NOS2)and Arg1 (arginase-1) in keratinocytes was accomplished by crossing mice (in a C57/Bl6J background ascertained by extensive backcrossing and SNP analysis) homozygous for the floxed allele in HIF-1α, HIF-2α, NOS2 or Arginase-1 into a background of Cre recombinase expression driven by the K14 promoter, which is specific to cells of the keratinocyte linage.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: The K14 promoter is specific to cells of the keratinocyte lineage.
source: Targeted deletion of Hif1a (HIF-1α), Epas1 (HIF-2α), Nos2 (NOS2)and Arg1 (arginase-1) in keratinocytes was accomplished by crossing mice (in a C57/Bl6J background ascertained by extensive backcrossing and SNP analysis) homozygous for the floxed allele in HIF-1α, HIF-2α, NOS2 or Arginase-1 into a background of Cre recombinase expression driven by the K14 promoter, which is specific to cells of the keratinocyte linage.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the K14 promoter.

claim: The NOS2 mouse was generated by Ozgene in C57Bl6 embryonic stem cells via homologous recombination, using placement of loxP sites flanking exon 3.
source: The NOS2 mouse was generated by Ozgene (Perth, Aus) in C57Bl6 embryonic stem cells via homologous recombination, and uses a placement of the loxP sites flanking exons 3.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: Cre recombinase-mediated deletion of the loxP-flanked exon 3 in NOS2 introduces a translational frameshift, rendering downstream exons non-functional.
source: Cre recombinase-mediated deletion of the loxP-flanked exon introduces a translational frameshift, rendering downstream exons non-functional.
evidence: This is a description of the molecular mechanism of the genetic modification.

claim: The probability of the data being best represented by two different models (mutant vs. littermate) was >99.99% in all cases analyzed by non-linear regression.
source: Non-linear regression modelling was undertaken, using a least squares method, with Akaike's Informative Criteria (AICc) used to determine whether the data could best be represented by a single model, or separate ones. The probablility of the data being best represented by two different models was >99.99% in all cases.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis results.
